title: Your CEO wants answers your dashboard can’t give
content:
A missed opportunity never shows up on the balance sheet. The customers we failed to understand, the products they would have bought, and the prices they would have paid — none appears as a line item. For the boardroom, they don’t exist and never did. Marketing’s costs are highly visible in the boardroom. When its contribution to business value remains unproven, marketing becomes an easy target for the first and hardest cuts.
The damage extends beyond budget cuts. Marketing has lost much of its mandate. Product moves to product management, price to sales, and place to channel, trade, and ecommerce teams. The CMO is left with promotion, tasked with generating demand for decisions made elsewhere.
Marketing’s understanding of the customer should inform all four Ps. Yet its dashboards largely measure promotional performance. Fast data helps optimize campaigns, while slow data connects customer needs to revenue, margins, and profit. Both are essential to guiding decisions that drive business value as AI accelerates execution.
Daniel Kahneman ’s distinction between fast, automatic thinking and slow, deliberate thinking offers a useful lens for understanding this gap. Marketing relies heavily on fast data.
Fast data creates relevance. Slow data provides meaning. Without that meaning, marketing can demonstrate more clicks and conversions while leaving revenue growth, margin, and profit unexplained. It’s like telling a story without a clue or plot.
AI makes this gap more urgent by accelerating analysis and execution. Without the customer understanding that gives those engines direction, marketing risks losing further influence across all four Ps. The CMO’s opportunity is to establish that understanding, prove marketing’s value, and reclaim a strategic role in the boardroom .

Which message works? Which button converts? Which interaction should come next? Fast data answers these questions. It shows what the customer is asking or doing now, helping marketing adjust campaigns, offers, and interactions. The dashboard shows the results: reach, traffic, leads, conversions, acquisition costs, and ROAS. These metrics help assess marketing performance.
But reach and traffic aren’t revenue. Leads and conversions aren’t revenue growth by definition. ROAS isn’t profit. The table below shows this gap: marketing can report improvement on the left without demonstrating improvement on the right.
Take ROAS. A campaign can generate more attributed revenue while discounts, product costs, and returns leave less profit. The dashboard may show a winning campaign even as the business earns less from each sale. Improving the reported return on advertising doesn’t automatically improve the company’s return.
Or take conversions. More customers buying once doesn’t tell us whether they’ll return, buy at full price, or cost more to serve than they contribute. A conversion records a transaction. Understanding its value requires looking beyond that moment.
Your CEO asks about revenue, growth, margin, and profit. If marketing answers with traffic, conversions, acquisition costs, and ROAS, the question remains unanswered.
Slow data starts on the right of the table above and reverse-engineers value. If the business needs higher margins, which customers and products contribute to them? Why do those customers buy? What makes them willing to pay full price? If the business needs revenue growth, where is the opportunity: acquiring customers, retaining them, or growing existing relationships?
Slow data supports value engineering: tracing how solving a customer’s problem creates value for the customer and the company. What outcome does the product deliver? What is that outcome worth to the customer? How does delivering it contribute to revenue, margin, or growth? These questions give marketing a basis for deciding what to promote, to whom, and why.
Slow data includes reflective analysis: questioning assumptions, interpreting behavior, and investigating how customers create value.

Slow data answers the questions the CEO needs to know. Who is our customer? What problem are they solving with our product? What is their lifetime value? What do they need to understand about our product, promotion, price, and place? Customers can’t always articulate what drives their decisions. We need to examine what they buy, how they use the product, when they return, and where their behavior differs from what they say.
Take the discount campaign above. Customers convert when the price drops. But why did they need the discount? They may have understood the product and waited for a deal. Or they may not have understood its value well enough to justify the full price.
The conversion looks the same in the dashboard. Value engineering asks whether lowering the price or better explaining the value produces a stronger outcome for both the customer and the company. It’s about understanding the fabric of your revenue.
Slow data isn’t new, but AI changes its value. As AI makes it easier to generate analyses, recommendations, and campaign variations, the constraint shifts from finding an insight to finding the insight that matters. Fast data contributes immediate context: what the customer is asking or doing now. Slow data provides the broader customer and business context needed to interpret those signals through deliberate thinking.
Take our discount example. At the moment level, a customer clicks an offer. At the session level, they compare products and delivery options. At the journey level, they appear ready to buy. These signals might suggest sending a promotion now. But the relationship context reveals that they recently bought the product at full price and still await delivery. Interpreting the immediate signals alongside that history changes the relevant action from selling to resolving.
The figure describes how context changes at different speeds. Slow thinking can examine any layer, including something that happened seconds ago. A service failure can change the customer’s circumstances immediately. Understanding what it means for the relationship requires reflection. The speed of the event and the thinking applied to it are different things.
For the CMO, the main task is to carry the value fabric into execution. If customers hesitate because they don’t understand the product’s value, that finding should shape campaign briefs, product pages, and the instructions given to AI. If repeat purchases drive profitable growth, acquisition campaigns should be assessed against returning customers and the value they contribute, as well as the first conversions they generate.
That also changes the brief we give AI. Prompting it to “increase conversions” leaves the business consequence open. Instead, asking it to “help customers understand the product’s value and increase full-price purchases” gives execution a customer problem and a commercial objective. We can then test whether better explanations improve purchases, margins, and returns. The dashboard measures progress against a reasoned objective.
AI will make the fast engines faster. Slow thinking helps establish what those engines should pursue and how to interpret their results. Can your organization explain what the customer is trying to solve and how serving that need creates business value? If it can, does that understanding actually guide your campaigns, dashboards, and AI?
